evals.prompt: I'm building an iPad reading app with a library, a storefront, and a settings area. Should I use a tab bar or a sidebar for the top-level navigation? It also runs on iPhone.
evals.expected_output: A platform-aware recommendation: on iPadOS consider the convertible tab bar (sidebarAdaptable) that switches between sidebar and tab bar; on iPhone (compact width) a tab bar with 3 top-level destinations. Reasoning grounded in HIG guidance (tab bars for 2-5 peer sections, sidebars for larger screens/hierarchies, collapse behavior at compact width).
assertions: Recommends a sidebar (or the convertible sidebarAdaptable tab bar) for iPad regular-width layouts
Recommends a tab bar for iPhone compact width
Grounds the recommendation in HIG guidance (peer top-level sections / larger-screen hierarchy) rather than personal taste

evals.prompt: What's the minimum tap target size for buttons in my watchOS app, and how should I style/arrange two side-by-side buttons at the bottom of the screen?
evals.expected_output: Cites watchOS hit-target values (44x44 pt default, 28x28 pt minimum control size), capsule-shaped buttons, and the side-by-side rule: equal heights with images or short titles; full-width buttons preferred for primary actions; toolbar placement for corner buttons.
assertions: States the watchOS hit target of 44x44 pt (28x28 pt minimum control size)
Describes watchOS buttons as capsule-shaped
States the side-by-side rule: two buttons need equal heights and images or short titles

evals.prompt: On iPhone my filter options open in a popover like on iPad but it looks weird. Should this be a sheet? What does Apple recommend for a quick filter UI on iPhone vs Mac?
evals.expected_output: Explains that popovers are for iPad/Mac and that on iPhone the same content should present as a sheet (or menu for simple option lists); platform-specific recommendation for iPhone vs Mac. Grounded in components-presentation.md (now part of the full corpus), which records the popover-adapts-to-sheet-in-compact behavior.
assertions: Recommends a sheet (or menu) instead of a popover on iPhone
States that popovers are appropriate on iPad and Mac
Does not fabricate HIG citations for content the skill's references don't cover

evals.prompt: My app hard-codes #FFFFFF backgrounds and a custom blue (#1E6EF4) for buttons. What do I need to change to support Dark Mode properly per Apple's guidelines?
evals.expected_output: Replace hard-coded hex with semantic/system colors (systemBackground sets, label colors); define custom brand colors as asset-catalog Color Sets with light/dark (and increased-contrast) variants; minimum 4.5:1 contrast (7:1 ideal); don't add an app-specific appearance toggle; mention base vs elevated dark backgrounds on iOS.
assertions: Recommends semantic/system background and label colors instead of hard-coded hex
Recommends asset-catalog Color Sets with light/dark variants for the custom blue
Cites the 4.5:1 minimum contrast ratio
Advises against adding an app-specific light/dark appearance toggle

evals.prompt: When should I use a pull-down button vs a pop-up button vs a context menu in an iOS app? I have a 'Sort' control and a per-item actions affordance in a list view.
evals.expected_output: Correct component mapping: pull-down = menu of actions related to the button's purpose; pop-up = mutually exclusive options with selection state (right for Sort); context menu = touch-and-hold on an item for its most-used commands (right for per-item actions), destructive items last/red, items duplicated in main UI.
assertions: Maps the Sort control to a pop-up button (mutually exclusive options with selection state)
Maps per-item actions to a context menu (touch and hold)
States the pull-down vs pop-up distinction: actions vs mutually exclusive options
Notes that context-menu items must also be available in the main interface

evals.prompt: Designing a new iOS app in 2026 — how should I handle the tab bar and toolbar materials? I keep hearing about Liquid Glass. What are the rules?
evals.expected_output: Current-era guidance: system tab bars/toolbars adopt Liquid Glass automatically — don't recreate or fight it; Liquid Glass belongs to the floating control layer, never the content layer; regular vs clear variants (clear only over rich media, with 35% dimming layer rule); tint one prominent button rather than many; monochromatic bars over colorful content; scroll edge effect rather than backgrounds.
assertions: States that system tab bars/toolbars adopt Liquid Glass automatically and shouldn't be recreated
Places Liquid Glass in the floating control layer, never the content layer
Distinguishes the regular vs clear variants (clear only over rich media)
Advises tinting at most one prominent control rather than many
